title: When aging meets digital & AI: Closing the silver digital divide for an aging world
gist: World Bank digital economists argue the collision of population aging and the AI/digital revolution creates a measurable but largely unmeasured 'silver digital divide': Thailand is nearly as aged as the U.S. (15% vs 18% over 65) yet only 52% of older Thais are online, about half the U.S. rate. They size the prize at a US$15 trillion silver economy by 2030 and 34 million potential eldercare jobs in East Asia and Pacific, and argue senior digital inclusion should be treated as core economic policy, not welfare.

insights.claim: Populations over 65 are growing not just in developed countries but across many middle-income economies, producing fewer workers, weaker demand, overstretched health systems and rising long-term fiscal sustainability risk.
insights.so_what: Middle-income sovereign credit stories increasingly hinge on aging-driven fiscal paths - a slow-burn rating and duration risk in EM Asia and Latin America.
insights.quote: overstretched health systems, and rising risks to long-term fiscal sustainability
insights.speaker: WBG_DigitalDev

insights.claim: Digital technologies including AI can now deliver at scale exactly the services aging societies need most - tutoring workers, guiding patients and delivering public services - which were previously scarce and costly.
insights.so_what: Positions AI service delivery as the supply-side answer to demographic decline, framing the addressable market as government and health budgets rather than consumer spend.
insights.quote: Digital technologies, including artificial intelligence (AI), can now deliver services once scarce and costly, from tutoring workers to guiding patients and delivering public services.
insights.locator: The second is the technology revolution
insights.speaker: WBG_DigitalDev

insights.claim: The core paradox is that older adults have the most to gain from digital technologies yet are among the least likely to access and use them, causing aging societies to forgo healthier lives, longer productive lives and reduced care costs.
insights.so_what: Identifies adoption rather than capability as the binding constraint - the investable gap is interface design, onboarding and assisted-use services, not new models.
insights.quote: The core paradox is that older adults have much to gain from digital technologies, yet they are often among the least likely to access and use them
insights.speaker: WBG_DigitalDev

insights.claim: Thailand is nearly as aged as the United States - 15 percent of its population over 65 against 18 percent in the U.S. - yet only 52 percent of older Thais are online, about half the U.S. level.
insights.so_what: The cleanest quantification of the divide: middle-income countries are aging at rich-country speed with half the digital readiness, concentrating the policy and product opportunity there.
insights.quote: Thailand is nearly as aged as the U.S., with 15 percent of its population over 65 against 18 percent in the U.S., yet only 52 percent of older Thais are online, about half the U.S. level.
insights.locator: For instance, Thailand is nearly as aged
insights.speaker: WBG_DigitalDev

insights.claim: Internet use among the working-age population aged 15 to 64 consistently exceeds that of adults 65 and above in almost every economy, and the divide extends across finance, health, work and public services.
insights.so_what: A universal rather than country-specific gap means age-friendly digital design is a globally scalable product requirement, not a localization niche.
insights.quote: This gap spans almost every economy: internet use among the working-age population (15 to 64) consistently exceeds that of adults 65 and above.
insights.speaker: WBG_DigitalDev

insights.claim: The overlap between aging and digital disconnection is most pronounced in middle-income countries where aging has begun or is about to accelerate while digital usage among older adults stays slow.
insights.so_what: Pinpoints where the pain arrives first - middle-income Asia faces the aging shock without the digital infrastructure buffer rich countries had.
insights.locator: The overlap between aging and digital disconnection
insights.speaker: WBG_DigitalDev

insights.claim: The silver digital divide remains largely unmeasured and overlooked in policy, with the authors describing the agenda as new and wide open.
insights.so_what: An admitted measurement vacuum from the institution that builds these indicators - expect new World Bank indices and country diagnostics, which typically precede lending programs.
insights.quote: silver digital divide remains largely unmeasured and overlooked in policy.
insights.locator: But the attention is not yet enough
insights.speaker: WBG_DigitalDev

insights.claim: In Thailand about a third of people aged 60 and above are still working, most in low-productivity self-employed jobs, while better-paid work increasingly requires the digital skills where older adults are furthest behind.
insights.so_what: Quantifies a trapped labor pool: reskilling older self-employed workers is a direct productivity lever with measurable output, not a social program.
insights.quote: In Thailand, for example, about a third of people aged 60 and above are still working, most in low-productivity, self-employed jobs.
insights.speaker: WBG_DigitalDev

insights.claim: Equipping older workers with AI and digital skills is argued to convert accumulated experience into higher productivity and new business formation, partially offsetting shrinking workforces.
insights.so_what: If correct, AI-enabled senior labor participation is a partial offset to demographic drag on potential GDP - a bull case rarely priced into aging-economy forecasts.
insights.quote: Equipped with AI and digital skills, older workers can turn experience into higher productivity and new businesses.
insights.speaker: WBG_DigitalDev

insights.claim: The divide is framed as permanent rather than generational: as technology keeps evolving every generation will need to keep learning, so today's digitally native cohorts will face their own version of the gap.
insights.so_what: Rebuts the common 'this solves itself as digital natives age' assumption - implies a durable, recurring market for adult retraining rather than a one-off cohort fix.
insights.quote: As technology evolves, every generation will need to keep learning.
insights.locator: This divide is not only about today's older adults
insights.speaker: WBG_DigitalDev

insights.claim: AI is already a major source of everyday health guidance with 230 million people asking health questions each week, positioning it for prevention and chronic care to relieve overstretched health systems.
insights.so_what: A hard usage number for consumer health AI - 230m weekly health queries is already primary-care-scale demand running outside the formal system and largely unmonetized.
insights.quote: AI is already a major source of everyday health guidance, with 230 million people asking health questions each week.
insights.locator: Relieving health systems and improving public services
insights.speaker: WBG_DigitalDev

insights.claim: Digital technologies are argued to let people age more healthily and independently while helping governments deliver better public services, easing the fiscal pressure that aging exerts on public finances.
insights.so_what: The fiscal-savings argument is what unlocks government budgets for eldercare tech - watch for it appearing in national aging strategies as a justification line.
insights.quote: Digital technologies can help people age more healthily and independently while helping governments deliver better public services.
insights.locator: Aging drives relentless demand for care
insights.speaker: WBG_DigitalDev

insights.claim: People aged 65 and above already hold about one-third of global wealth, fueling a silver economy expected to reach US$15 trillion by 2030.
insights.so_what: A one-third wealth share with below-average digital participation is the largest under-served consumer segment in digital services - the mismatch is the opportunity.
insights.quote: people aged 65 and above already hold about one-third of global wealth
insights.speaker: WBG_DigitalDev

insights.claim: In East Asia and the Pacific alone, meeting unmet eldercare needs could create 34 million jobs by 2030.
insights.so_what: Eldercare is one of the few named large-scale job-creation channels in aging Asia - relevant to labor policy, migration flows and care-services operators.
insights.quote: In East Asia and the Pacific alone, meeting unmet eldercare needs could create 34 million jobs by 2030.
insights.speaker: WBG_DigitalDev

insights.claim: Closing the divide creates new markets for age-friendly digital and AI solutions by enabling older adults to participate more fully in the digital economy, making inclusion an investment rather than a transfer.
insights.so_what: Reframing inclusion as market creation is how the spending gets financed - supports commercial rather than donor-funded product categories in eldertech.
insights.quote: creating new markets for age-friendly digital and AI solutions
insights.locator: Addressing this disparity can unlock this potential
insights.speaker: WBG_DigitalDev

insights.claim: Korea became a super-aged society in 2024 with people aged 65 and above accounting for one-fifth of its population, and has responded with nationwide digital literacy programs and in-person 'digital helpers' stationed where older adults frequently go.
insights.so_what: The most advanced live policy template; countries aging faster than they digitize will import Korea's playbook, creating demand for physical assisted-onboarding services alongside software.
insights.quote: Korea aged rapidly and became a super-aged society in 2024, with people aged 65 and above accounting for one-fifth of its population.
insights.speaker: WBG_DigitalDev

insights.claim: Korea's programs demonstrate that digital skills can be learned at any age, undercutting the assumption that older-adult non-adoption is an immovable behavioral constraint.
insights.so_what: If adoption is trainable rather than fixed, the addressable market for senior digital services is far larger than current usage rates imply.
insights.quote: These programs show digital skills can be learned at any age.
insights.speaker: WBG_DigitalDev

insights.claim: The prescribed agenda is to measure the gap country by country, design digital tools and public services around how older adults actually live, and treat senior digital inclusion as core economic policy rather than a welfare add-on.
insights.so_what: A three-step policy checklist likely to shape World Bank digital-development lending conditions - an early indicator of where technical assistance money flows next.
insights.quote: treating senior digital inclusion not as a welfare add-on but as core economic policy for aging societies
insights.locator: Closing it will require deliberate work
insights.speaker: WBG_DigitalDev
